item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,304 as five die in 24 hours
item.description:
Five more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Friday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,304 .
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all five of the latest casualties as suspected .
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,199, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 105, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours .
Among the five new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in the Sylhet division with three deaths.
A total of 1,271 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Friday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 245,562 .
During the same period, 148 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 25,028 .
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 219,247 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 210,401 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS .

item.title: Bangladesh waits longer for offshore oil, gas exploration
item.description:
Bangladesh may have to wait at least two more years to begin offshore oil and gas exploration, as an extension of the bidding deadline is likely to delay the selection of companies and signing of contracts.
The deadline for submitting bids under the 2026 offshore bidding round has been extended to March 31 next year from November 30 this year. After bids are submitted, evaluation, negotiations and contract finalisation could take until late 2027, according to sources familiar with the process.
Even after contracts are signed, exploration cannot begin immediately. Companies will need to mobilise vessels and equipment and wait for favourable weather conditions at sea.
Experts say offshore exploration is largely weather-dependent. The sea is generally calmer between October and March, making it easier to operate exploration vessels. Rough conditions during the monsoon months, from April to September, make offshore operations difficult.
If the contract process continues until late 2027, companies may miss the next exploration season. In that case, work could be pushed back to the following favourable window, meaning exploration is unlikely to begin before October 2028.
The delay comes as domestic gas production continues to decline and Bangladesh becomes increasingly dependent on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG) to meet demand.
The government extended the bidding deadline following requests from potential investors, who sought more time to prepare their proposals. The issue was discussed during a recent London visit by the state minister for energy, who also chairs the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA).
The bidding round, launched on May 24 this year, offers 26 blocks in the Bay of Bengal — 11 in shallow waters and 15 in deep waters. The government has revised several terms, including gas pricing and tax concessions, under a new production sharing contract (PSC) to attract foreign companies.
Turkish Petroleum Overseas Company (TPOC) and China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) have purchased bidding documents. Several other companies, including Beringia Power Bangladesh, KrisEnergy, Pial Engineering and Construction, Onoda Inc, Rystad Energy and Max Infrastructure, have also purchased data.
A Petrobangla official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the deadline extension was necessary due to limited interest and requests from companies. The official expressed hope that the process would eventually attract bids, despite the delay.
Energy expert BD Rahmat Ullah said Bangladesh was already years behind in offshore exploration and would need at least five to seven years to obtain gas even if exploration began now.
He warned that the latest extension could push the country further behind, while neighbouring Myanmar was reportedly extracting gas from the same maritime region.
Energy expert Shamsul Alam blamed corruption in the energy sector for the delays, alleging that companies had faced demands for shares from people associated with the previous government, discouraging investment.

item.title: Gold, smartphones worth Tk1.13C seized at Dhaka airport
item.description:
The Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID) seized gold bars weighing 471 grams, 35 smartphones and other goods worth around Tk 1.13 crore in three separate drives at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on Thursday.
The seizures were made during the operations conducted by the CIID’s A-shift team, following increased vigilance against smuggling and customs duty evasion through passenger baggage, according to a press release issued on Friday.
In one operation, 171 grams of gold bars, along with cosmetics, food items and medicines, were recovered from the baggage of passenger Md Abul Hossain, who arrived in Dhaka from Bangkok on a US-Bangla Airlines flight.
The seized goods were estimated to be worth Tk 35.70 lakh.
In another drive, customs officials recovered 300 grams of gold bars, 35 smartphones of Samsung, Honor and Realme brands, 36 kg of soap and 6.375 kg of cosmetics from the baggage of passenger Shah Alam Aziz.
He arrived from Bangkok on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight.
After allowing 100 grams of gold under passenger baggage facilities, subject to payment of applicable duties and taxes and the required passport endorsement, officials seized the remaining excess gold and other goods.
The seized items were valued at around Tk 55.30 lakh.
In a separate search of the baggage of another passenger, Umma Hani, arriving on the same Biman flight, officials found 200 grams of gold bars and 40.48 kg of soap.
After allowing 100 grams of gold under baggage facilities, the customs officials seized the remaining gold and excess goods, valued at approximately Tk 21.77 lakh.
The CIID said the increasing number of attempts to bring gold and smartphones in small consignments pointed to an emerging smuggling risk at the airport.
Although individual consignments may appear relatively small, their cumulative impact could result in substantial revenue losses, it said.
The directorate is also examining whether such incidents are linked to organised smuggling networks.
The CIID said it had strengthened intelligence surveillance and intensified operations to counter changing smuggling methods and protect government revenue.

item.title: Bank account freezes rattle business community
item.description:
Businesses are facing mounting pressure amid sluggish investment, high interest rates, rising production costs and political and economic uncertainty. The National Board of Revenue’s (NBR) move to seek bank account details of more than 200 individuals and companies, and freeze accounts of around 100 people over alleged involvement in fuelling unrest in the garment sector, has added to entrepreneurs’ concerns.
Business leaders warn that indiscriminate account freezes based on political affiliations or past business ties could harm innocent entrepreneurs. They argue that action should be taken only after investigations establish specific evidence of involvement in labour unrest.
The NBR has started unfreezing accounts of some companies after the restrictions disrupted routine operations, including opening letters of credit (LCs), accessing bank loans and paying workers’ wages. However, uncertainty remains as investigations continue, with the revenue authority seeking transaction records covering the past five years from several businesses.
On November 4, the NBR’s Income Tax Intelligence and Investigation Unit and Central Intelligence Cell sent letters to banks seeking information on the accounts of more than 200 individuals and entities. Banks were also instructed to freeze the accounts of around 100 individuals.
NBR officials said the measures were taken based on intelligence agency information. The list reportedly includes former Awami League lawmakers and politically affiliated individuals, as well as businesspeople without known political connections.
Several major export-oriented groups have also come under scrutiny. The accounts of 28 companies under Mondol Group were sought, while those of its chairman Abdul Momin Mondol, managing director Abdul Alim Mondol and several others were frozen. The group exported around $560 million worth of garments in the 2025-26 fiscal year and employs about 50,000 workers.
Companies under Well Group, Envoy Group, Standard Group, Tusuka Group, Nipa Group and Givenchy Group have also come under the NBR’s scrutiny.
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) has raised concerns with the government, seeking to prevent further complications for the industry.
BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan Babu said the association had urged the government not to freeze the accounts of factory owners or companies without specific evidence that they had instigated or financed labour unrest.
He said the association was continuing discussions with the government and expected the accounts of those against whom no specific allegations had been established to be released promptly after verification.
Following discussions, the NBR has unfrozen the accounts of several companies, including those under Sheltech Group and Standard Group. Some accounts belonging to Mondol Group and Envoy Group companies have also been released, although those of several individuals remain frozen.
Businesspeople say lifting the restrictions does not fully resolve the problems. The freezes have already complicated LC openings, access to approved credit facilities and other financial transactions. Such incidents could also damage companies’ reputations among foreign buyers, they warn.

item.title: RMG workers to get rice at Tk30 per kg
item.description:
A special Open Market Sale (OMS) programme offering rice at Tk30 per kg to readymade garment (RMG) workers was launched on Friday to ease their living costs and ensure access to affordable food.
Under the programme, each worker can purchase up to 10kg of rice a month at the subsidised rate, according to a handout from the Press Information Department (PID).
Initially, rice is being sold through 66 truck-sale points across Dhaka city, Savar, Dhamrai, Gazipur, Narayanganj and Chittagong.
Each truck carries five tonnes of rice, with a total of 330 tonnes being sold every Friday. The programme will continue until further notice.
Of the daily allocation, Gazipur receives the largest share at 150 tonnes through 30 truck points, followed by Narayanganj and Chittagong with 50 tonnes each through 10 points. Savar receives 40 tonnes through eight points, Dhaka city 30 tonnes through six points and Dhamrai 10 tonnes through two points.
Sales take place in two shifts every Friday: 10am to 12:30pm and 2:30pm to 5pm, subject to stock availability.
Workers must show their factory identity cards and sign a master roll to purchase rice under the programme.

item.title: Govt eyes electric train services on Dhaka-Chittagong route
item.description:
The government plans to extend electric train services to Chittagong after launching a pilot project on the Narayanganj-Dhaka-Joydebpur corridor as part of efforts to modernise the country's railway network.
The expansion would bring electric trains to the busy Dhaka-Chittagong route, improving passenger services, speeding up freight transportation and reducing dependence on fossil fuels.
Bangladesh Railway Chief Planning Officer Engineer Md Rafiqul Islam said the government plans to introduce electric multiple-unit (EMU) trains capable of running at speeds of up to 140kph.
The pilot project has received approval from the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC), with an estimated cost of Tk3,500 crore. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is expected to provide most of the financing, while the government will cover domestic costs, including duties and VAT.
The tendering process is expected to be completed by 2027, with major construction work scheduled to progress from mid-2028.
A total of 16 EMU train sets will be imported for the pilot corridor. The trains will have driving facilities at both ends, allowing them to operate without being turned around.
Rafiqul Islam said the Dhaka-Chittagong corridor was a priority because of its importance for passenger and freight movement, connecting the capital with the country's main seaport and commercial centres.
Currently, only 60,000-70,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) of containers are transported annually by rail from Chittagong to Dhaka, accounting for around 3% of total container traffic.
The Dhirashram Inland Container Depot project aims to increase annual rail container transportation to 450,000 TEUs, creating scope for greater freight movement by rail.
To support railway electrification, Bangladesh Railway is also developing infrastructure along key routes. Construction of the third and fourth railway lines between Dhaka and Tongi is progressing, while double-line construction on the Tongi-Joydebpur section has been completed.
Additional land is being acquired at Joydebpur for an EMU depot and workshop. Meanwhile, metre-gauge lines on the Tongi-Akhaura and Laksam-Chittagong routes are being converted into dual-gauge double lines.
Rafiqul Islam said Bangladesh Railway was prioritising electric trains capable of running at 140kph rather than bullet trains, which can reach speeds of around 350kph.
Introducing bullet trains would require an estimated Tk150,000-250,000 crore, alongside major land acquisition and other challenges in the country's densely populated landscape, he said.
Electric trains are also expected to reduce carbon emissions, air pollution and fuel consumption. Bangladesh Railway is assessing the potential environmental benefits and opportunities to earn carbon credits through internationally recognised mechanisms.
The pilot corridor is expected to lay the groundwork for a wider electric railway network, with Chattogram identified as the next major expansion destination.

item.title: IEA: Global oil supply to surpass demand in fourth quarter
item.description:
Global oil supplies are expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter, after increased Gulf exports led to a market surplus in October for the first time since the Iran war, the International Energy Agency said Friday.
Even though attacks on tankers trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz have continued, Gulf shipments reached 18.4 million barrels per day (mb/d) -- though that was still 26% below pre-war levels, the Paris-based agency said in its monthly report.
“The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the IEA said.
Prices have fallen sharply in recent weeks as more vessels prove willing to make the risky transit through the Strait of Hormuz under US escort.
Iran effectively closed the crucial strait in the early months of the war launched by the United States and Israel in late February.
That helped overall oil supply to rise by three million barrels per day in September and a further 2.3 million barrels in October, the IEA said.
But global demand is set to fall by 2.7 mb/d overall this year as oil prices remain well above pre-war levels and “accelerate electrification and fuel efficiencies across the global car fleet.”
Diesel prices in particular stood at $180 per barrel in October, around 77% higher than before the war, as Iran struck refineries in neighboring Gulf countries accused of aiding US attacks.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and other energy installations are also disrupting diesel supplies to the global market.
“The severe tightness in product supply, especially for diesel, remains the overriding concern of the broader market and consumers,” the IEA said.

item.title: Humanitarian situation in Gaza worsens amid political deadlock
item.description:
This autumn’s heavy rain and falling temperatures are exacerbating the humanitarian situation for civilians in Gaza. Torrential rainfall over the weekend killed at least six people, including children, according to Unicef. Local authorities said at least 70,000 tents were flooded and more than 200,000 people affected.
“Over the past two days, we have been trying to stabilize our tent with sand and rubble to keep water from seeping inside,” Rawan Al-Omari, a mother of two, told DW on the phone.
She and her children share a tent west of Jabalia in northern Gaza. “The entire area around us has turned into mud, so even leaving the tent has become difficult,” the 33-year-old said. “Everything is exhausting.”
The rain also soaked the tent and everything 45-year-old Radi Amin and his three children own.
“For three consecutive days, we have been trying to dry our clothes while my children were shivering in the cold,” he told DW. “Only on Wednesday, with the sun finally out and warm enough, our belongings started to dry.”
Amin said that “the heavy rain served as a stark reminder of our truly dire state.”
Aid teams meanwhile have started to clear blocked sewer lines and stormwater basins at 60 locations, benefiting an estimated 30,000 families, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) reported on Wednesday.
However, Ocha’s humanitarian partners also warned that there is not enough space to relocate people living in flooded areas or war-damaged buildings. “Israeli authorities are restricting Palestinian access anywhere behind the so-called ‘Yellow Line,’ which means that most of Gaza’s land remains off limit,” Ocha said.
Following the Hamas resistance campaign against Israel on October 7, 2023, the ensuing war in Gaza has destroyed most of Gaza’s infrastructure and housing. More than 74,600 people were killed in the Gaza Strip, according to figures from Gaza’s Health Ministry. Israel controls about two-thirds of the territory, which is marked by a military demarcation line, the so-called Yellow Line.
Hamas continues to exercise governing authority in much of the remaining territory close to the Mediterranean Sea, where most of Gaza’s roughly 2 million residents live. Most of them have been displaced several times and live in tents, camps for displaced people or in houses that are deemed unsafe.
As part of the US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025, US President Donald Trump established the Board of Peace (BoP) committee to oversee the ceasefire’s implementation as well as Gaza’s postwar governance and reconstruction. According to a joint assessment by the World Bank, United Nations and European Union published in April 2026, Gaza’s recovery and reconstruction will require an estimated $71.4 billion (€64.2 billion) over the next decade.
However, little progress has been made as negotiators have been failing to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its troops from the territory. Despite the ceasefire, Israel continues to carry out airstrikes on Gaza. On Thursday, Israel carried out a strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis against alleged Hamas members.
For Nathan Brown, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University in the US, the current rainfall exemplifies the deadlock of Trump’s peace plan for Gaza.
“The failure of the Board of Peace to advance reconstruction, or even secure reliable relief, is fundamentally due to Israeli objections based on the insistence that Hamas has to completely disarm first,” he told DW.
Until the recent elections in Israel, the Board of Peace showed little interest in challenging that view, Brown added: “Now it is willing to go public, though not in very confrontational terms.”
On Monday, the Board of Peace issued a statement saying that Israel’s steps to improve the humanitarian situation ahead of the coming winter remain insufficient. “We call on the leadership of the current Government of Israel to act immediately to authorize and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterization and humanitarian supplies.”
Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (Cogat) said the same day that among other equipment, 12 sewage vacuum trucks for the International Committee of the Red Cross arrived in Gaza and that 91,000 tents and more than 8,200 trucks carrying tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothing had entered Gaza in recent months.
In its statement, the Board of Peace also called on Hamas to abide by commitments under the ceasefire, including laying down its weapons and transferring governing authority. Hamas promptly rejected the criticism in a statement and accused Israel of obstructing implementation of the peace plan and withholding urgently needed humanitarian supplies.
The United Nations as well as numerous international agencies have accused Israel of systematically preventing the import of prefabricated shelters into Gaza. The UN said around 150,000 tents were outside Gaza and ready to be dispatched, pending the necessary approvals, a claim Israel rejects.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is serving as caretaker prime minister while a new government is being formed following the October 27 elections, denied that Israel was responsible for the worsening conditions and blamed Hamas instead.
He warned that “as long as Hamas remains in power, it will use every dual-use item entering Gaza to entrench its terror regime and expand its military arsenal.”
For Gaza’s population, this deadlock amid the approaching winter spells ongoing hardship.
“Children and families are facing devastating conditions, with around 1.2 million people, including more than 560,000 children, living in critical or catastrophic shelter conditions,” Ahmad Alhendawi, regional director of the aid organization Save the Children, told DW.
The amount of available winter clothing remains critically insufficient in Gaza, he added.
“As available supplies cover less than 1% of needs, hundreds of thousands of children face the winter without adequate clothing, blankets or heating, leaving them exposed to hypothermia and respiratory illnesses,” Alhendawi said.
Furthermore, Nestor Owomuhangi, the UN Population Fund’s (Unfpa) representative to Palestine, told DW that around 400,000 people in Gaza continue to live in areas at high risk of flooding, including an estimated 10,000 pregnant women.
“For women and girls already enduring displacement and hunger, the rain threatens their health, safety and dignity,” he told DW, adding that “with around 180 babies born every day, mothers and newborns urgently need dry, warm shelter.”

item.title: Law minister: Govt has information on network behind crude bomb, arson attacks
item.description:
Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman on Friday said the government had obtained information and evidence about those involved in a network behind recent crude bomb explosions and arson attacks, adding that several people had already been arrested.
“We have obtained all the information and evidence about who is involved in this network and how they are connected,” he said while addressing a special meeting of the Dhaka-based Jhenaidah Journalists' Forum at the National Press Club in the city.
The minister urged journalists to examine who was behind the acts of violence and identify those involved in the attacks.
Referring to attempts to create fear through crude bomb explosions and arson attacks, he said those involved in such activities did not understand the people of Bangladesh.
He said the people would not allow the ousted fascist and authoritarian regime to regain political space or engage in terrorism in the country.
The law minister also expressed confidence that Bangladesh's economic, political and social progress would continue and that the country would maintain its growing stature on the global stage.
He urged journalists to report on the basis of accurate information and evidence, stressing that they should not hesitate to publish reports even if those went against him or the government.
“We want to move forward on the right path based on accurate information from you,” he said.
He also called upon journalists to report both the government's shortcomings and its positive initiatives, saying they should highlight efforts to ensure people's rights alongside reporting against injustice, corruption and drug abuse.
He said the government was ready to cooperate with journalists in their efforts to combat yellow journalism and uphold the dignity of the profession.

item.title: Trump official seeks $50 billion for air traffic control after outage
item.description:
USA-AVIATION/

The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $50 billion late Friday after a communications issue forced a nationwide groundstop that halted thousands of flights for hours.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and the White House earlier on Friday asked for $30.1 billion to upgrade the United States' aging airports and air traffic control system.

"This is an emergency," Duffy said. "What's more important than having an air traffic control system that actually works?"

The issue impacted the FAA's en route centers that handle traffic between airports. But the Republican-led Senate Commerce Committee said the incident highlights the need to prioritise modernising those centers over other projects and noted Congress approved $1.9 billion to replace outdated en route centers.

The world's most complex airspace has experienced a series of events in recent years that have disrupted flights and risked safety. In January 2025, a midair collision at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport killed 67 people.

Congress already approved $12.5 billion over five years in July 2025 to upgrade air traffic control and increase the hiring of controllers following complaints about airport ​congestion, flight delays and technology ​problems.

The request from White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy seeks $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization, including $7.2 billion for a common automation platform and controller workstations and $2 billion for cloud computing.

"This investment is critical to complete the modernisation of our national airspace - delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Vought wrote to lawmakers asking for swift action.

Major airlines including American Airlines AAL.O, Delta Air Lines DAL.N, United Airlines UAL.O and Southwest Airlines LUV.N have expressed support for the request.

The $30.1 billion request also includes $2 billion to replace and improve Federal Aviation Administration air traffic control towers and $18 billion for airport-related projects including $10 billion to modernise or replace aging terminals.

The FAA relies on decades-old ​computers as well as replacement parts bought through auction websites. Last week, it said it would replace by the end of 2028 floppy disks used for weather and other critical information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities.

Vought and Duffy in their letter said the FAA has replaced 68 per cent of legacy copper telecommunications network with high-speed fiber infrastructure.

The administration has called for the Republican-led Congress to approve funding in the final weeks of the year. Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January.

In September, the dual failures of a circuit at a Philadelphia ​air traffic facility and the ​accidental severing of a ⁠fiber-optic cable in New Jersey by a construction crew led to thousands of flights across the densely populated Northeast being delayed or canceled.

item.title: Trump, Xi, Putin to hold historic meeting in China, what’s on the agenda
item.description:
APEC-SUMMIT/TRILATERAL-MEETING

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday.

Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, US officials said.

The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.

One of the major conflicts dominating Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the US officials said.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.

Tesla and Space X boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but won't be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.

Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday , their fourth meeting since the US president's return to power last year.

But Trump is not scheduled to have a separate one-on-one with Putin.

Among other topics, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy is not expected to come up in Trump's meetings with Xi, the officials said.

"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," a second US senior official said.

The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.

Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before heading to Shenzhen.

Fifth shipment of uranium arrives at Rooppur plant
item.description:
The fifth shipment of uranium fuel for the second unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Pabna arrived at the project site early Saturday, marking another step towards the plant's commissioning.
The fuel, sourced from Russia, was transported to the plant in three specialised lorries at around 5:30am under tight security.
Members of the Bangladesh Army and other law enforcement agencies provided security during the transportation.
According to project sources, six shipments of uranium fuel have reached the site so far: one for the first unit and five for the second unit.
Under the delivery plan drawn up by Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom, 163 uranium fuel assemblies are scheduled to be delivered for the second unit through seven cargo flights. Another 48 assemblies are planned to arrive in two separate cargo shipments as reserve fuel for the first unit. This will bring the total number of shipments to nine.
Meanwhile, preparations for commissioning the plant's first unit are also underway. The unit is currently in the "Power Start-up Stage-C" phase, for which the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) Chairman granted approval on October 29.
During this phase, the reactor's power output will be gradually increased to test the performance of various plant components, including turbines, generators and safety systems.
Once the tests are completed successfully, the generator of the first unit will be connected to the national power grid in a process known as synchronization.
According to the project plan, the first unit is expected to supply around 300 megawatts of electricity to the national grid on a trial basis in November. However, the start of trial power generation will depend on the completion of the necessary tests and approval from the regulatory authority.
Built with Russian technology, the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant comprises two units equipped with VVER-1200 reactors. Once fully operational, the plant is expected to significantly boost the country's power generation capacity and strengthen long-term energy security.

item.title: Climate pledges fall short as Bangladesh seeks $11bn annually
item.description:
Bangladesh has urged developed countries to accelerate climate finance delivery, saying it needs between $10 billion and $11 billion annually to address the impacts of climate change, as international funding commitments continue to fall short of the needs of vulnerable nations.
The country is already spending an estimated $4.5 billion to $5 billion annually from domestic sources on climate-related initiatives, highlighting the scale of investment required to strengthen resilience and support its transition to a lower-carbon economy.
The demand was raised at a press briefing by the Bangladesh delegation on Thursday during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, where climate finance remains a central issue in negotiations between developed and developing countries.
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo said the progress made in pledging climate finance had not been matched by the actual delivery of funds.
The delegation called for more accessible international financing, particularly grant-based support, arguing that complex approval procedures and delays in disbursement were preventing vulnerable countries from responding effectively to climate risks.
Foreign Affairs State Minister Shama Obaed Islam stressed that financial assistance must reach communities facing the greatest climate threats rather than remain tied up in lengthy funding processes.
Responding to a question from Carbon Brief about Bangladesh's expectations from the climate finance work programme, a delegation representative said greater clarity was needed on funding responsibilities and distribution mechanisms.
The representative also highlighted the challenges facing communities displaced by river erosion, underscoring the need for financing arrangements that can respond to the immediate needs of climate-affected populations.
Bangladesh's demands reflect broader concerns among least developed countries (LDCs) over the widening gap between climate finance commitments and the resources available to implement adaptation measures.
In its written statement, the delegation backed the LDC Group's call for a threefold increase in adaptation finance to $120 billion annually before 2035.
It urged developed countries to meet their existing climate finance commitments and expand grant-based assistance, particularly to support the implementation of National Adaptation Plans in climate-vulnerable countries.
Bangladesh also called for simplified and more direct access to the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility and the Adaptation Fund.
The delegation supported an LDC proposal to establish a platform connecting national adaptation priorities with potential funders and development partners, aiming to bridge the gap between countries' climate plans and their implementation.
On the Global Goal on Adaptation, Bangladesh said the proposed Belém Adaptation Indicators should provide a meaningful way to measure progress in climate resilience without introducing additional reporting requirements for developing countries.
It also called for greater financial and technical support for locally led adaptation, recognising the importance of community-level initiatives in responding to climate impacts.
Bangladesh raised concerns over the limited resources available to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, saying its existing financing was insufficient to meet demand from submitted proposals.
The delegation called for increased financial contributions, simplified direct-access arrangements and faster disbursement to countries experiencing the consequences of climate change.
It also stressed that funding should address both economic losses, such as damage to infrastructure and livelihoods, and non-economic losses, including displacement and damage to cultural and social assets.
The written statement further said Bangladesh was among the first five countries expected to receive $30 million each from the Climate Investment Funds.
Coastal infrastructure and climate-resilient agriculture were identified as priority areas for the expected financing.
The delegation also raised concerns over unilateral climate-related trade measures, including the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
It warned that such measures could place additional pressure on businesses, workers and exporters in developing countries, potentially undermining their economic development efforts.
Responding to questions about whether the issue should feature in a COP31 decision, a delegation representative argued that countries that had benefited from activities contributing to the climate crisis should also take responsibility for supporting those most affected.
The representative said climate policies should not create additional trade barriers for developing economies already facing the costs of climate impacts and the transition to cleaner production.
Journalists also questioned whether COP negotiations included dedicated financing to protect children and safeguard their education in climate-vulnerable countries.
A delegation representative said they were not aware of any specific financing demand exclusively dedicated to children, while referring to ongoing efforts to strengthen healthcare services.
On the broader question of benefits for vulnerable communities, the delegation said international negotiations had helped establish climate change as a shared global challenge and encouraged countries to develop action plans, although implementation remained a major challenge.
Bangladesh accounts for less than 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions but has reaffirmed its commitment to reducing emissions under its updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).
The country has pledged to reduce emissions by 6.39% below its business-as-usual projection by 2035 using domestic efforts, with a further 13.92% reduction conditional on receiving international support.
The delegation backed extending the Mitigation Work Programme through 2030, calling for sector-specific action supported by adequate financing, technology transfer and capacity-building.
It also stressed that the transition to a low-carbon economy must be just and inclusive, prioritising least developed and other climate-vulnerable countries while protecting employment, expanding skills development and providing social protection for affected workers and communities.
Bangladesh said it would continue coordinating with the LDC Group, the G77 and China, and other international partners during the second week of COP31 to push for stronger outcomes on climate finance.
For Dhaka, the central challenge is no longer simply securing new financial pledges but ensuring that promised resources reach countries and communities facing the consequences of a crisis they have contributed relatively little to creating.
This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organised by Internews' Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

item.title: Dhaka ranks world's third most polluted city Saturday morning
item.description:
Dhaka, the densely populated capital of Bangladesh, ranked third among the world’s most polluted cities on Saturday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 195 at 9:14am.
The city’s air was classified as "unhealthy", indicating a health threat, according to the AQI report.
India’s Delhi, Pakistan’s Lahore and India’s Kolkata occupied the first, second, and fourth spots on the list, with AQI scores of 235, 232, and 192, respectively.
According to the AQI scale, a reading between 50 and 100 is considered "moderate", with generally acceptable air quality, though sensitive individuals should limit prolonged outdoor exertion. AQI levels of 101–150 are "unhealthy for sensitive groups", 151–200 is "unhealthy", 201–300 is "very unhealthy", and readings above 301 are considered "hazardous", posing severe health risks.
The AQI, which reports daily air quality, informs residents how clean or polluted the air is and highlights potential health effects. In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five key pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution. Air quality usually deteriorates in winter and improves during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that air pollution causes about seven million deaths worldwide each year, primarily from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: UN climate chief urges debt-free climate finance for developing nations
item.description:
UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell has called for a fundamental shift in the global climate finance system, urging developed countries, financial institutions and investors to ensure that funding helps developing nations escape mounting debt pressures and build long-term economic resilience.
Speaking at the Seventh Biennial High-Level Ministerial Dialogue on Climate Finance at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on Friday, Stiell warned that many developing countries remain trapped in a cycle of debt, climate disasters and increasingly expensive borrowing, leaving them with fewer resources to protect their people and economies.
“Climate finance must help countries break free,” he said, stressing that meeting international funding targets alone would not necessarily address the actual financial needs of vulnerable nations.
He argued that climate finance must move beyond funding individual projects towards supporting broader economic transformation, strengthening national institutions and creating conditions that attract more investment at lower costs.
Under the new climate finance goals agreed at COP29, developed countries are expected to take the lead in providing $300 billion annually by 2035, while all actors are expected to work together to scale up financing for developing countries from all sources to $1.3 trillion per year by the same year.
Stiell said the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap provides a pathway towards achieving these targets, but stressed that the way climate finance is delivered must change to make the commitments meaningful.
Explaining the financial challenges facing developing countries, Stiell said the growing threat of floods, wildfires, storms and droughts increases borrowing costs even before disasters occur.
When climate shocks strike, government revenues decline while recovery and reconstruction expenses rise, pushing countries further into debt.
This leaves governments with fewer resources to invest in climate adaptation, resilience and low-emission development, reinforcing a cycle of financial vulnerability.
To break this cycle, he called for climate finance that reflects individual countries' economic circumstances and debt sustainability.
He emphasised that funding must be affordable and tailored to national needs rather than delivered through a one-size-fits-all approach.
While private finance, loans and guarantees remain important for meeting global climate goals, he said grants and highly concessional financing would continue to be essential, particularly for least developed countries (LDCs), small island developing states (SIDS) and other vulnerable economies.
He also called for broader international efforts to address debt burdens so that developing countries are not forced to choose between repaying loans and investing in climate resilience.
Stiell identified easier access to climate finance as another major priority, pointing to the complicated administrative requirements and fragmented funding arrangements that developing countries must navigate.
He said countries often face complex procedures to access funding from multiple programmes and institutions, making it difficult to secure resources when they are needed.
“We need procedures simplified,” he said, calling for stronger coordination among financial institutions and reduced administrative burdens.
He also stressed that international climate finance should align with national development priorities rather than requiring countries to reshape their domestic systems to meet external funding requirements.
National treasuries, local governments, development banks and financial institutions already play important roles in financing development, and these institutions should be strengthened rather than bypassed, he said.
Stiell urged international partners to invest in institutional capacity and help developing countries establish effective systems to access, manage and deploy climate finance.
He also underscored the importance of developing and transferring technologies that support climate-resilient and low-emission development.
The UN climate chief further called for stronger cooperation among governments, climate funds, development banks, financial institutions and private investors to turn national climate plans into tangible investments.
He said climate finance, technology transfer and capacity-building must work together around countries' own priorities, ensuring that funding translates into projects that strengthen resilience and improve people's lives.
As an example, he explained that early grant-based support could help countries build institutional capacity and develop investment pipelines, while concessional finance and risk-sharing instruments could subsequently help projects expand.
He said international climate negotiations and cooperation mechanisms could play an important role in bringing different sources of finance together around national development priorities.
Concluding his remarks, Stiell called for a new approach to international climate finance, saying the biennial ministerial dialogues should help translate commitments into more effective delivery.
Established in 2013, the dialogues have contributed to discussions on global climate finance. However, he said they must now help advance a system that supports long-term development rather than focusing solely on individual funding targets.
“Where every dollar invested in development builds a better future. For all countries,” he said.
His remarks at COP31 highlight a central challenge for developing countries such as Bangladesh: securing not only greater volumes of climate finance but also affordable, accessible and predictable funding that can strengthen economic resilience without deepening existing debt pressures.
